How DMAR Counts and Requires Bootstrap Replications

Source: R/dmar_bootstrap.R
dmar_bootstrap.Rd

One rule governs every DMAR function that reads an interval, a bound, a reference quantile, a standard error, or a Monte Carlo p-value from B bootstrap or Monte Carlo replications: how many replications the request must ask for, what happens to a replication that returns no value, what the result records, and when no interval is reported. This page states the rule and its reasons; each function's page says how the rule applies to it.

How many replications an interval needs

A percentile limit is a quantile of the B replications, so it is located by the replications that lie beyond it. With B = 100 and a 95 percent interval there are two or three of them on each side, and the limit moves with every new seed. DMAR runs an interval read from quantiles only when the number of replications requested puts at least 10 beyond each limit, and never from a request of fewer than 100: 200, 400, and 2,000 replications at the 90, 95, and 99 percent levels. The count is held to the number requested, B; what happens when some of them return no value is decided afterward and is described under Replications that return no value. In symbols, with \(t\) the smallest tail area a reported limit cuts off (\((1 - C)/2\) for a two-sided interval at level \(C\)), $$B_{\mathrm{required}} = \max\{100, \lceil 10 / t \rceil\}.$$ With 10, the share of the bootstrap distribution a limit actually cuts off has a relative standard deviation of about 30 percent whatever the shape of that distribution (a nominal 2.5 percent is between about 1.2 and 4.5 percent in 95 of 100 runs, depending slightly on how the quantile is interpolated). How far the limit itself moves depends on the shape: with 400 replications at the 95 percent level its standard deviation from run to run is about 0.13 bootstrap standard errors for a bell-shaped distribution, about 0.20 for one with tails as heavy as a t distribution on 5 degrees of freedom, and about 0.29 on the long side of a skewed one. Ten is a floor and not a recommendation. The defaults (1,000 where each replication refits a model, 2,000 to 10,000 elsewhere) put 25 to 250 replications beyond each limit at the 95 percent level, and at 1,000 the standard deviation of a limit of a bell-shaped distribution is about 0.08 standard errors. A BCa interval needs more, 1,000, 2,000, and 10,000 at the three levels, for the reason given under BCa intervals. An interval built from the standard deviation of the replications ("bootstrap_se") is reported from 100, at which that standard deviation has a coefficient of variation of about 7 percent for a bell-shaped distribution (12 to 14 percent for the heavy-tailed and the skewed shapes above), and a Monte Carlo p-value from 100, at which its standard error is at most 0.05. A request below the number required is refused before anything is computed, with a condition of class dmar_count_invalid that states the number. None of these numbers concerns the coverage of the bootstrap for a given statistic, which no number of replications repairs; they limit only the error added by drawing a finite number of resamples. The numbers in this paragraph were computed for DMAR by simulation (20,000 runs each); the statement about the share cut off follows from the Beta distribution of an order statistic (the tail area beyond the \(k\)-th of \(B\) ordered draws from a continuous distribution is distributed as Beta(\(k\), \(B - k + 1\))). No published source is cited for the counts.

A limit at quantile position \(p\) has the tail area \(\min(p, 1 - p)\). For an interval with unequal tail areas (alpha_lower and alpha_upper of the ratio functions and of ci_eta_squared_generalized) the smaller area decides; for a one-sided bound (htmt) and for a reference quantile (parallel_analysis, factor_count) it is the area beyond that one quantile, so a bound at the 95th percentile needs 200 replications and one at the median needs the floor of 100.

The functions that compute their limits directly read them with quantile (its default, type 7); the reliability family and ci_bifactor_indices read them with boot::boot.ci(), which places a limit at the \((B + 1)\alpha\) position among the ordered replications. The two differ by a fraction of the distance between adjacent replications.

Replications that return no value

A resample can leave a statistic undefined (a constant variable, a model that does not converge, a denominator of zero). Such a replication is dropped and counted, never replaced. Every result records B (requested), B_used (the number the interval rests on), n_dropped, and B_required (the fewest replications a request may ask for) as attributes, which dmar_metadata returns, with bootstrap_status, and one warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped states the counts. An interval from the replications that remain describes the resamples in which the statistic is defined. When the dropped replications number at least the share of the distribution beyond one limit (2.5 percent of B for a 95 percent interval), they could by themselves decide where that limit falls, and the warning says so (caution is TRUE in the condition). When more than half were dropped no interval is reported: the limits are NA, the estimate is returned, and the warning has class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. The call does not stop for this, so an estimate that took minutes to compute is kept. With more than half dropped a larger B does not help: the replications that remain are a minority of the resamples, selected by whether the statistic could be computed, and their spread describes those resamples and not the sampling distribution of the estimate.

The number required is counted on the request and not on the replications that remain. A request of exactly 400 at the 95 percent level from which 3 replications are dropped reports its interval from the 397 that remain, with the warning. The two rules about shares, in the paragraph above, then decide: more than half dropped withholds the interval, and dropped replications that reach the share beyond one limit bring the caution. The warning states how many were dropped, and when those that remain are fewer than the number required it says so and says to request more. Where replications can fail (a model refit in every resample, sparse categories, a small sample), ask for more than the minimum, so that the limits rest on at least the number the rule intends; the defaults do.

bootstrap_status is one of "complete" (nothing dropped), "dropped" (some dropped, the interval formed), "exploratory" (formed from a request below the required number, under the option described below), "insufficient_count" (no interval: a BCa interval whose adjusted positions take more replications than were requested, or fewer than two usable replications), and "insufficient_share" (more than half dropped, no interval). With several statistics in one call (the pairs of htmt, the effects of mediation_mbco, the coefficients of mlmr), B_used is the smallest count any reported limit rests on and n_dropped is B - B_used. Where a table already has rows for the counts it keeps them (mediate has rows B and B_used, krippendorff_alpha the row B_used); the reliability family keeps its fuller bootstrap attribute, which gains required and bootstrap_status.

BCa intervals

The BCa interval reads its limits from quantiles that the bias correction and the acceleration move away from the nominal ones. For a 95 percent interval the positions might be 0.9 and 99.1 percent in place of 2.5 and 97.5, and the limit at 0.9 percent has few replications beyond it. The count of 10 is applied where each limit finally sits, again to the number of replications requested, so a BCa interval can be withheld after the replications are run (warning of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient, with the positions and the count that would have served). To make that uncommon, a BCa interval is run only with 50 replications beyond each nominal limit: 1,000, 2,000, and 10,000 at the 90, 95, and 99 percent levels. In simulations of an indirect effect and of a correlation at the 95 percent level, the adjusted positions asked for more than 2,000 replications in at most 14 percent of data sets (an indirect effect with 50 cases and small paths) and in 0 to 3 percent of the others, and for more than 10,000 in about 1 percent of the data sets of that hardest condition and in none of the others (400 data sets per condition).

When the bias correction or the acceleration is itself undefined (a leave-one-out estimate that cannot be computed, every replicate on one side of the estimate, influence values without spread), the functions differ by family. mediate, cohen_kappa, and fleiss_kappa refuse the BCa interval with an error of class dmar_bca_undefined whose message names the cause; ci_ratio_of_means and ci_ratio_of_means_paired stop with an error that names ci_method = "percentile"; the reliability family and ci_bifactor_indices report the percentile interval in its place, with a warning, and record the substitution in the ci_method attribute.

Fewer replications, for exploration

A first look at an analysis, a help page example, and a simulation that averages over many data sets do not need a reportable interval from each run. options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) lets a function run with any B of 2 or more. Nothing else changes: the result still records B_required, its footer says that the interval is below the requirement, and every call gives a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_exploratory. A planner that runs B replications inside each of many simulated studies (ss_aipe_indirect_effect, ss_aipe_indirect_effect_sensitivity, ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity) gives the warning once for the call and records the request (B_used is then B, the number each simulated study ran), and plot_mediation_mbco, whose result is a plot, gives the warning and records nothing. The share rules still apply. An interval obtained this way is not one to report. Set the option for the calls that need it and restore it afterward:

old <- options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE)
mediate(d, x = "x", m = "m", y = "y", B = 50, seed = 113)
options(old)

Monte Carlo intervals and reference quantiles

The same rule holds for limits read from the quantiles of Monte Carlo draws (ci_method = "monte_carlo" of mediate and of mediation_mbco, the band of plot_mediation_mbco) and for the reference quantile of parallel_analysis and factor_count, with "draw" or "reference data set" in place of "replication". The Bollen-Stine p-value of sem_exact_fit_bootstrap is a proportion and not a quantile: it needs a request of 100 samples, is withheld when more than half were set aside, and is reported with the Wilson interval of its own Monte Carlo error.

What is not a bootstrap

The rule does not govern n_resamples of randomization_test, randomization_test_paired, and procrustes_phi, or the number of simulated studies G of the sample size planning and sensitivity functions. Those counts are checked as counts and their functions report their own Monte Carlo error.

Reproducibility

Every function that draws replications has a seed argument (boot_seed in mlmr and mlmr_mv) that defaults to NULL: the replications are then drawn from, and advance, the current random number stream. A supplied seed is set for the call only and the caller's generator state is restored when the function returns, so a reproducible call does not disturb the random numbers of the script around it. Two runs with the same seed and the same B give the same limits; the same seed with a different B does not.

Conditions

dmar_count_invalid

Error (a dmar_refusal). B is not a single whole number of at least the number required. Fields arg, min (the number required), max, and reason (the sentence that explains the number).

dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped

Warning. Replications were dropped and the interval was formed from the rest. The message states how many, and says to request more when those that remain are fewer than B_required. Fields B, B_used, n_dropped, B_required, share_dropped, caution, and status.

dmar_bootstrap_insufficient

Warning. No interval is reported: more than half of the replications were dropped (status "insufficient_share"), or the adjusted positions of a BCa interval take more replications than were requested, or fewer than two replications were usable ("insufficient_count"). The same fields; for a BCa interval withheld at its adjusted positions also positions (the two positions, as proportions) and B_suggest (one and a half times the count those positions take, rounded up to a hundred).

dmar_bootstrap_exploratory

Warning. The result was computed from fewer replications than a reported result needs, because options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) is set. The same fields as the dropped warning.

dmar_bootstrap_note

Warning. Something else about the run that the reader of the interval should know, with every replication used and the interval formed: in the reliability family and ci_bifactor_indices, a BCa interval replaced by the percentile interval (the ci_method attribute records the substitution), or replicates that all have the same value, so that the interval has no width; in average_variance_extracted and parallel_analysis, the function's account of a run in which nothing was dropped (replications from an improper solution that were kept, reference data sets whose fits gave warnings). The same fields as the dropped warning where the function records them.

dmar_bca_undefined

Error (a dmar_refusal). The bias correction or the acceleration of a BCa interval is undefined (mediate, cohen_kappa, fleiss_kappa).

The warnings of the reliability family and of ci_bifactor_indices, which share one bootstrap engine, begin with the name of the function that was called ("reliability_omega(): ") and carry that name in the field fun; reliability passes its call on, so its warning names the function that ran the bootstrap. A program can muffle or read any of the warnings by class:

withCallingHandlers(
  mediate(d, x = "x", m = "m", y = "y", seed = 113),
  dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped = function(w) {
    message(w$n_dropped, " of ", w$B, " dropped")
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  })

The functions the rule governs

"Required" is the fewest replications a request may ask for at the 95 percent level (for the reference quantiles, at the 95th percentile). Kind Q reads quantiles, S takes a standard deviation of the replications, and P is a Monte Carlo p-value.

the same functions: BCaQ, BCa100002000the same
the same functions: "bootstrap_se", "bootstrap_se_logistic"S10000100the same
reliability_omega_categoricalQ, BCa, or S10000 (1000 under missing = "mi")400, 2000, or 100under multiple imputation each replication is imputed several times

The planning functions ss_aipe_indirect_effect, ss_aipe_indirect_effect_sensitivity, and ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity run an interval inside each simulated study; their pages state the inner B they use.

References

Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An introduction to the bootstrap. New York, NY: Chapman & Hall/CRC. (For the percentile and BCa intervals themselves, as the function pages cite it. The counts on this page are not taken from it.)
